newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends lower; but Nasdaq, bonds, dollar rise.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends lower; but Nasdaq, bonds, dollar rise.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks snapped a three-day record-breaking rally to end lower on Thursday, but the Nasdaq set another all-time high and bonds rose for a fourth day in a row as investors awaited Friday's key July employment report.
The dollar rose.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 32.28 points to 8,222.61.
But the broader market was firm. Continued strength in market-leading computer and financial stocks pushed the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks and the Nasdaq composite index to fresh highs.
The S&P 500 rose 2.00 points to 954.29 and the Nasdaq composite finished up 5.76 to 1,593.81.
On the New York Stock Exchange, advancing issues outnumbered declines by a ratio of 1,716 to 1,145 on volume of 547.8 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Market players linked the Dow's drop to profit-taking by investors wary of the release on Friday of the July U.S. payrolls, wages and employment report ahead of the stock market opening.
"I think the lack of enthusiasm is because of waiting for tomorrow morning's release," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/Twenty-First Advisers.

Economists expect, on average, for the report to show the economy created 193,000 new jobs in July, compared with 217,000 in June. The unemployment rate is expected to dip to 4.9 percent from 5.0 percent in June.
The market will also get the July report from the National Association of Purchasing Management on Friday.

Stronger-than-expected data could derail the rally in stocks and bonds by raising inflation fears. But some analysts said the recent wave of economic news showing mild growth and subdued inflation reduces the chances the market will be blindsided by the reports.

"These things weigh a lot less on our minds now that there's such a preponderance of evidence that the economy's growing at a strong rate without inflation pressure," said Robert Robbins, market strategist at Robinson-Humphrey Co.

On Thursday, the government reported that the gross domestic product expanded at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the April-June second quarter, less than half the revised 4.9 percent pace in the first quarter.
A key inflation measure in the GDP report -- the implicit price deflator -- edged up 1.4 percent in the second quarter after a 2.4 percent first-quarter rise.

The inflation-sensitive bond market extended its rally, with the 30-year Treasury up 12/32, or $3.75 on a $1,000 bond, reducing its yield to 6.30 percent from Wednesday's 6.33 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
In late New York trade, the dollar was quoted at 1.8385 marks vs. 1.8370 marks late on Wednesday, and at 118.65 yen, up from 118.41 yen.
Soybean prices rose strongly on reports of strong export demand and forecasts for more dry weather in the Midwest as soybeans head into a key stage of growth.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November rose 24-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $6.58. Corn was buoyed by the rally, with December corn ending up 4-1/4 cents a bushel at $2.67-3/4.
In New York, silver prices rose on positive sentiment about future demand from jewellers and other fabricators, helping the metal buck fresh negative sentiment about gold.
Silver for September delivery at the COMEX closed 11.7 cents higher at $4.490 an ounce, breaking out of the range of $4.20-4.40 seen for the past three weeks.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,907.5, down 19.8 points, or 0.40 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,331.43, up 118.61 points, or 0.59 percent.
